transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Um, well, I guess I came in because... I don't know, it's my mind. It just keeps going completely blank on me, and it's happening at the absolute worst possible times. I work as a flagger and a crossing guard—I actually have a bachelor's degree, but this is what I've been doing for years now, so you'd think it would all be second nature to me by this point. You know, you stand out there, you manage the traffic, you keep the road crews and the pedestrians safe. It’s a huge responsibility. But lately, I’ll just be out there on the asphalt, and... it's like someone just unplugs my brain. 

I will literally look at the road-closure forms I have to fill out, or I'll be standing there holding my stop-slow paddle, the exact same paddle I've used every single day, and suddenly I just cannot remember the steps. I can't remember what I'm supposed to do next. It's just empty up there. Steps I have done for years, just completely gone. And it's so terrifying because you have cars coming at you, and you have to make these quick decisions to keep traffic flowing safely, but I'm just standing there staring at the paddle trying to force my brain to process what it means, and it just... it won't. I just freeze because there's nothing in my head.
During these episodes when your mind goes blank, do you notice things like your heart racing, sweating, or trouble breathing, or do you ever lose awareness of what's happening around you?

No, it's not like that. I mean, my heart isn't pounding out of my chest or anything. I'm not gasping for air or hyperventilating. I know some people get like that when they're stressed at work, especially out on the road with all the exhaust and the heat and the angry drivers, but for me, physically... my body feels completely normal. I'm not sweating any more than I usually would be, standing out in the blazing sun in a thick high-vis vest and steel-toed boots, you know? 

And I definitely don't lose awareness of what's happening around me. Honestly, that is almost the worst part of the whole experience, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. I am completely, painfully aware of every single thing going on. I can see the F-150 rolling up too fast, I can see the heat waves coming off the asphalt, I can hear the road crew drilling fifty feet behind me. I'm just trapped inside my own head, looking out at all of it. It’s like my eyes are working perfectly, my ears are working perfectly, but the control room up here is just... empty. 

Like last Tuesday—or maybe it was Wednesday, we were doing a lane closure over on 4th street—I was just standing there, breathing totally fine, heart rate totally normal, but I was watching this woman in a silver Honda staring at me through her windshield, waiting for me to flip the sign. And I knew she was there. I was fully aware of her existence, and the road, and the fact that I was holding a sign, but I just couldn't connect the dots on what I was supposed to actually do about it. So no, I'm not passing out or having a panic attack or forgetting where I am. I know exactly where I am. I just... the instructions are just completely gone.
When one of these episodes happens, about how long does it usually last before your mind starts working normally again—seconds, minutes, or longer?

Um, I don't really know, to be honest. It's so hard to judge time when you're just standing there in that state, you know? Like, when you're out on the road, time is already a weird thing. Sometimes a ten-hour shift feels like two days, and sometimes you blink and it's time for lunch. But when this happens... when my brain just unplugs like that... I can't really tell you if it's been thirty seconds or three minutes. 

It feels like an eternity, I can tell you that much. Like, going back to that woman in the silver Honda... I was just staring at her, and she was staring at me, and I could feel the sun beating down on the back of my neck—it was one of those really humid days where the air just feels heavy, you know? And I'm just standing there, holding the paddle, and it felt like we were locked like that for an hour. But it couldn't have been an hour, obviously, because the traffic would have backed up all the way to the interstate, and the foreman would have been screaming at me over the radio. But I don't know exactly how long it actually was. 

Maybe it was just a few seconds? Or maybe a minute? I really couldn't say. I just know that eventually, somehow, it kind of... clicks back on. Like an old TV warming up. The instructions sort of float back into my head, and I realize, oh, right, I need to turn the paddle to 'slow' and wave her through. But the actual duration of the blankness? I have no idea. I'm sorry, I wish I could give you a better answer, a more exact timeframe, but I just... I don't have one. It's just a chunk of time where I'm physically present but mentally just... gone.

During these episodes, have you or anyone else ever noticed you making any involuntary movements—like lip-smacking, fumbling with your hands, or repetitive gestures—or has anyone told you that you looked 'out of it' or unresponsive even though you felt aware?

No, I haven't noticed anything like that, and no one has ever mentioned it to me. I mean, I'm pretty sure I'd know if I was smacking my lips or fumbling around. I'm just standing there holding the paddle, you know? It's a pretty big paddle, too—it's not like a little sign, it's on a long pole, so both my hands are usually occupied with that. And like I was saying before, I'm completely aware of everything going on around me. I can feel the weight of the pole in my hands, the grip of my gloves... I'm not doing any weird repetitive gestures. I'm just frozen. 

And as for people telling me I look 'out of it'... well, honestly, most of the time the drivers aren't really paying that close attention to my face anyway. They're looking at the sign, or they're looking at their phones, or they're just glaring because they're annoyed they have to stop. And the road crew is usually busy doing their own thing, drilling or pouring asphalt or whatever. I mean, maybe someone has looked at me and thought I seemed a little spaced out for a second, but no one has ever actually come up to me and said, 'Hey, you looked really unresponsive back there.' 

The foreman hasn't said anything. The other flaggers haven't said anything. It's just... it's all internal. It's just my brain stopping. But physically, outwardly? I think I just look like a flagger standing there holding a sign. Just... maybe standing there a little too still for a few seconds too long. But no, no weird movements or anything like that. Just the blankness in my head.
Do these blank spells tend to happen more when you're feeling especially stressed, anxious, or under pressure, or do they seem to occur randomly regardless of how you're feeling at the time?

Well, see, I’ve spent a lot of time trying to figure that out myself. Because you'd think it would be stress, right? Road work is inherently stressful. But it doesn't really feel like I'm having a particularly anxious day and *then* it happens. It's more like... it just happens at the absolute worst possible times, almost like a cruel joke. 

And honestly, that is the whole reason I finally made this appointment and came in here to see you. Because my mind just keeps going completely blank at the exact moments I need it to work the most. Like, I will be looking at the daily road-closure forms—and these are standard forms, I have filled them out literally hundreds of times. With my background, you'd think a simple closure form wouldn't be an issue, and it never was before. But I'll be staring at the clipboard, or I'll be out there holding the stop-slow paddle, just doing the routine, and suddenly... I just cannot remember the steps. Steps I have done for years! 

It’s all just wiped clean. I’m standing there staring at the paperwork, or staring at this piece of reflective aluminum on a stick, trying to force my brain to remember what comes next, and the knowledge is just... not there. And that *causes* stress, obviously. When you're standing there and the foreman needs the forms signed off so the concrete trucks can move, or when you have a line of commuters tapping their steering wheels, you feel the pressure. But the anxiety comes *after* the blankness, not before. 

Before it happens, I'm usually just doing my job. I'm just existing. And then, bam, the instructions are gone. It's so incredibly frustrating because it makes me look incompetent to the rest of the crew, and I'm not. I've been doing this for years. So I guess to answer your question, the blankness itself seems to just hit me randomly, regardless of how I'm feeling. It just always manages to pick the exact moment I can least afford for it to happen.
After one of these blank spells ends and your mind 'clicks back on,' do you feel completely normal right away, or do you feel tired, foggy, or need a little time to fully get back to yourself?

Oh, no, it’s completely immediate. There’s no fog, no tiredness, nothing like that at all. It’s literally just... boom, I’m back. Like I said before with the old TV analogy, once the picture is there, it’s just there in full color. I don't need to sit down or splash water on my face or take a minute to get my bearings. 

Which is a good thing, honestly, because out on the road, you really don't have the luxury of taking a minute. If you're foggy out there, if you're sluggish, somebody gets run over or a cement truck backs into a trench. So when I snap back, I am instantly at a hundred percent again. Like with that lady in the silver Honda I was telling you about... the very second my brain plugged back in and I remembered I was holding the paddle, I didn't feel groggy in the slightest. I just instantly flipped the sign from 'stop' to 'slow' and gave her the wave to move forward. Now, my heart was pounding, sure, but that was just from the sheer panic of realizing I had been standing there like a statue, not because my body was physically exhausted or my head was cloudy. 

It’s the exact same thing with the closure forms. One second I'm staring at the clipboard like it's written in ancient Greek, and the next second, the English language just returns to my brain and I sign the bottom line and hand it back to the foreman. I don't need a nap, I don't have a headache, my vision isn't blurry. I just pick up exactly where I left off. 

It's almost more jarring that way, to be honest with you. Because if I felt tired or sick afterward, at least I'd have a tangible excuse, right? I could tell the crew, "Oh, man, I'm feeling really under the weather today, I got dizzy for a second," and they'd understand. But I don't. I feel completely fine physically. I'm just standing there in my high-vis vest, totally alert, perfectly awake, just... trying to seamlessly re-enter the flow of traffic and pretend like I wasn't just completely checked out of my own head. And I'll tell you, that takes a lot of mental energy, having to constantly cover up the fact that my brain keeps dropping the signal. But the actual physical feeling right after it happens? No, no fog at all. I'm just instantly back to normal.
Can you think back to when these blank spells first started—was there anything significant going on in your life around that time, like a stressful event, loss, or major change?

Well... yes. I’ve actually spent a lot of time trying to trace it all back to day one, trying to figure out exactly when the switch flipped. Because you always want to know where things begin, right? If you can find the source of a leak, maybe you can figure out how to patch it. So I’ve gone over the timeline in my head a thousand times, looking at the calendar, looking back at my old work schedules and trying to pinpoint the exact moment my brain started doing this. 

And it’s been going on for about a year and eight months now. And the reason I know that timeline so specifically, down to the month, is because of what happened right before it all started. You asked about a loss, and... yeah. My closest friend died. Just right before all this blankness began. 

We were incredibly close. We actually met back when I was getting my bachelor's degree, and we had been through everything together since then. You know how you have that one person who just anchors you? The person who just inherently understands how your mind works? When you lose that, the whole world just shifts on its axis. I remember the exact season she passed, because the road crew was just transitioning into the fall paving schedule, and I had to take time off for the funeral. It was just devastating. 

And when I finally came back to work after that... that's when I first noticed the signal dropping in my head. The blank spells. It's been a year and eight months of this, and honestly, it feels like an absolute eternity to be dealing with this on top of everything else. But at the same time, the loss feels like it just happened yesterday. The grief just lingers, it sits heavy right on your chest, you know? And I keep thinking, maybe if she were still here, I wouldn't be standing on the highway forgetting how to read a standard closure form. Because she was always the one I talked to to decompress after a long shift. When she passed away, it left this massive, gaping hole in my life that nothing else can fill. 

So, yes, a year and eight months. Right after I lost her. I really think the two things have to be connected, because the timing is just too perfectly aligned for it to be a coincidence. I mean, one week my life is normal, the next week she's gone, and then suddenly my brain is just hitting the pause button on me. It has to be related to losing her, it just has to be.

Aside from these blank spells, have you noticed other symptoms since your friend passed—like trouble sleeping, intrusive memories or thoughts about her, or avoiding places and activities that remind you of her?

No, I... I wouldn't say that. Not like what you're describing. Like, with the sleeping thing? My sleep is always kind of all over the place anyway, just by the very nature of the job. When you're a flagger, you're completely at the mercy of the construction schedule. Sometimes we have night work because the city won't let them shut down the highway during peak daylight traffic hours, so I'll be out there from 9 PM to 5 AM standing under those massive, blinding halogen light towers. And then two weeks later, I'll get moved to a residential paving job that strictly runs 7 AM to 3 PM because of local noise ordinances. So my internal clock has been completely wrecked for years. If I have trouble falling asleep, it's usually just because my body literally doesn't know what time it is, not because I'm lying awake having nightmares or anything like that. 

And as far as avoiding places... no, definitely not. Honestly, it's almost the exact opposite. We lived in the same city for so long, we went to school together, so practically every square inch of this town has some kind of memory attached to it. If I started avoiding places that reminded me of her, I literally wouldn't be able to leave my apartment. I'd have to quit my job, because we used to drive these same roads all the time. Actually, I still go to the diner we used to eat at every single Sunday. It's this little place off Route 9, nothing fancy at all, but they have the best hash browns. We used to sit in the exact same booth in the back corner by the window. I still go there, and I still sit in that same booth. The waitress, Brenda, she still gives me this really sad, sympathetic smile when she brings the coffee because she knows I'm there alone now. But I don't avoid it. It actually feels nice to be there, in a way. 

So I don't really have those... what did you call them, intrusive memories? It's not like a sudden flashback or something jarring that forces its way into my head and scares me. It's not like that at all. It's just a constant, quiet missing her. It's just a heavy feeling that's always sort of sitting there. I'll be out on the road, holding my sign, and I'll see a car that looks like hers, or I'll hear a song on a passing car's radio that we used to listen to, and I just feel sad. But it doesn't interrupt my thoughts or make me panic or anything. It's really just these blank spells, where the signal just completely shuts off. That's the only really bizarre thing that's been happening. Everything else is just... you know, normal grief, I guess you'd call it. Just trying to figure out how to exist in a daily routine where she isn't around anymore. But no, no avoiding things or sudden bad memories keeping me awake.
Do these blank spells ever happen outside of work—like at home, while driving for yourself, or in casual conversations—or have you only noticed them happening on the job?

Well, I mean... I’ve thought about that a lot. Because, think about it—if I’m just at home, right? If I'm sitting on my couch watching Jeopardy or folding laundry, and my mind goes blank... who cares? Like, maybe it does happen there. Maybe I just sit there staring at the wall for a minute or two and I don't even realize it's happening, because there's no consequence to it. If I'm driving my own car to the grocery store and I zone out, maybe I just miss my turn and have to take the next exit. It's no big deal, you just loop around. 

But the whole reason I actually came in here to see you, the reason I finally picked up the phone and made this appointment, is because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst possible times. Like, the highest-stakes moments you could possibly imagine. I know I already brought up the road-closure forms and the stop-slow paddle earlier, but you really have to understand the context of it. I have been doing this job for years. Years. It is pure muscle memory at this point. You stand there, you flip the paddle, you make eye contact with the driver, you wave them through. Or with the closure forms at the end of the shift, it's just the same exact boxes every single time—date, time, location, foreman's name, signature. It's so basic. 

But then, out of nowhere, I will look at the road-closure forms or the stop-slow paddle, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I have done for years. It's like someone just reached into my brain and wiped the hard drive completely clean. I'll just be standing there on the asphalt, looking at this piece of paper or holding this sign, and for the life of me, I have absolutely no idea what it means or what I'm supposed to do next. The knowledge just completely evaporates. 

And when you're standing in a live lane of traffic, with a line of cars stretching back a quarter mile, and people are getting impatient and leaning on their horns... that is not the time to forget how to do your job. It's terrifying, honestly. It's a massive liability. So, maybe it happens at home, I really couldn't say for sure because there's no pressure there to snap me out of it or make me notice. But the work stuff? That's why I'm here. Because forgetting the most basic steps of my job while I'm standing in the middle of a highway... I just can't keep trying to hide that.

Do these blank spells only happen with certain specific tasks—like filling out the closure forms or holding the stop-slow paddle—or have you noticed them happening with other routine work tasks as well?

Right, exactly, like I was just saying about the forms and the paddle. That is exactly what I mean. I came in today specifically because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times, and it's just... it feels like it's spreading to everything. 

You asked if it’s other routine things, and... yes, it is. It's the radio, too. We use these heavy-duty two-way radios to communicate with the other flagger at the opposite end of the work zone, or with the pilot car driver. It's a very specific rhythm—you have to wait for the channel to clear, press the button on the shoulder mic, wait a second for the repeater to beep, and then speak. I've done it ten thousand times. But lately, I’ll reach up to my shoulder, and my hand will just freeze. I’ll stare at the radio, and I literally cannot remember how it works. Or setting up the advance warning signs, the big orange diamond ones. I'll be standing by the side of the road with the sign stand, and the sequence of how to unfold the legs and lock the cross-bracing just completely escapes me.

But the paddle and the forms... those are the ones that really scare me the most, which is why I keep bringing them up. Because like I was telling you, I will look at that stop-slow paddle, or I'll be holding the clipboard with the road-closure forms at the end of a long shift, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I have done for years. It's not just being distracted or being tired. It’s like the filing cabinet in my brain that holds the instructions just completely vanishes. I’ll look at the octagonal shape of the sign, I’ll see the red background, and my brain just refuses to connect it to the action of turning my wrist to show it to traffic. It’s a total void. 

And having that happen at the worst possible moments, with angry commuters flying by... I just can't afford to have my brain deleting steps I’ve known how to do for years. I'll just be standing there, completely empty-headed, trying to force my brain to remember how to be a flagger. It's just not safe, and it's exhausting to try and hide it from the foreman.
During these blank spells, do you ever feel detached from your own body or like you're watching yourself from outside, or that the world around you feels unreal or dreamlike?

No, I... I don't think so. I mean, I know what you're talking about, like in movies when someone goes through something intense and they suddenly float up to the ceiling and look down at themselves, or everything goes all blurry and slow-motion? It's really not like that at all. I am very, very much in my own body. 

If anything, I'm almost hyper-aware of being in my body because I'm standing there panicking on the inside. I can feel the exact weight of my steel-toe boots, you know? I can feel the sweat dripping down the back of my neck under my hard hat, and I can smell the diesel exhaust from the excavators, and that really sharp, chemical smell of the hot mix asphalt... it's all incredibly real. Too real, honestly. The world doesn't feel like a dream at all. The cars flying past me at sixty miles an hour definitely don't feel like a dream—the wind they kick up practically knocks you over if you aren't bracing your legs right. 

So I'm definitely grounded right there on the pavement. It's just... it's more like a computer freezing up. You know when you're working on something and suddenly the screen just stops responding, but the monitor is still on and the power is still connected and you can see everything perfectly fine, but you just can't click on anything? That's what it is. I'm looking right out of my own two eyes, and everything around me is sharp and loud and exactly where it should be, but the... the internal mechanism that tells me what to do next just completely halts. So, no, definitely no floating around or feeling disconnected from reality. I'm right there in the dirt and the noise. I just... I just don't know what I'm supposed to be doing while I'm standing there.

Right before one of these blank spells starts, do you ever notice a brief warning sign—like a strange smell or taste, a feeling of déjà vu, or a sudden odd sensation—that tips you off that it's about to happen?

No, God, I wish there was. I really, really wish there was some kind of warning, because if there was, maybe I could actually do something about it, you know? If I had even a five-second heads-up, I could step back from the fog line, or I could grab my radio and tell the other flagger, "Hey, cover my lane for a second, I need to step away." But I don't get that luxury. 

You asked about smells or tastes... I mean, out on the highway, you smell absolutely everything all day long. You smell the fresh hot tar, the diesel exhaust from the dump trucks, someone's burning brake pads coming down the hill, or just the stale coffee in my own thermos. It's a sensory overload out there. But there's never any *strange* smell right before it happens, or any weird taste in my mouth. It's just the normal, everyday smells of a heavy construction zone right up until the exact second my brain decides to pull the plug. 

And as for déjà vu? No, not at all. Honestly, it's almost the exact opposite of déjà vu. Because déjà vu is when you feel like you've been somewhere or done something before, right? But with this, it's like... I *have* been there a thousand times. I've stood on that exact patch of asphalt all week. But when the blank spell hits, suddenly it's like I've *never* been there. It's not a warning sign, it's just the spell itself hitting me like a ton of bricks. 

There's just no build-up whatsoever. One second I'm totally fine, I'm watching a silver Honda Civic coming up the lane, I'm calculating their speed, I'm checking my footing on the gravel, I'm thinking about whether I need to flip the paddle to 'Stop' or keep it on 'Slow' based on what the pilot car is doing... and the very next second, nothing. Just a totally empty room in my head. No weird tingling, no stomach dropping, no sudden chill. It's literally just like a light switch being flipped off without anyone even touching the dial. Which is exactly why it's so incredibly dangerous! If I just had a warning, I could manage it. But because there's absolutely nothing tipping me off... I'm just completely at its mercy out there.

Aside from these work-related blank spells, have you ever noticed gaps in your memory for other important personal information—like details about your own past, your relationships, or things that happened around the time of your friend's death—that you couldn't otherwise explain?

No, no, not at all. My memory for my actual life is... well, it is perfectly intact. If anything, it is almost too good, honestly. I don't have any missing time or blank spots when it comes to who I am or where I came from or the people in my life. I can remember my entire past with absolute crystal clarity. I can tell you the exact layout of my childhood bedroom, the weird floral pattern on the wallpaper, the way the floorboards creaked right outside the door. I remember every little detail about my relationships, even the things I would probably be much better off forgetting. I can remember arguments from ten years ago word for word, the exact tone of voice, the weather outside that day, everything.

And as for my friend... no. God, no. I wish I had gaps in my memory about that. I really do. Because I remember every single excruciating second around the time they died. I remember the exact moment I found out. It was a Tuesday, late afternoon, maybe 3:15 or so, and the light was coming through the living room blinds at this very specific, harsh angle. I was holding a mug of coffee that had gone completely cold, just staring at the wall when the phone rang. I remember the funeral, the suffocating smell of the lilies in the room, which is a smell I still absolutely cannot stomach to this day, and the scratchy fabric of the dark blue dress I was wearing. Every single detail of that time is permanently burned into my brain. There are absolutely no gaps there. 

So it really is just the work tasks. That is why it is so incredibly frustrating to me. My personal life, my history, the people I have loved and lost, all of that is perfectly filed away right where it belongs. I know exactly who I am. It is just the procedural stuff, the actual mechanics of doing my job on the site, that suddenly gets wiped. I will be standing out there on the asphalt, perfectly aware of my entire life story and every tragedy I have ever lived through, but I just cannot for the life of me remember how to operate a two-way radio or flip a stop-slow paddle. It makes absolutely no sense.

I'm not entirely sure what you mean by that, to be perfectly honest. Or maybe I just haven't ever experienced it, so it's not really clicking for me. But no, I haven't noticed anything like that at all. 

Like I was just saying, I try to be incredibly observant about my own body and my mind, especially lately. When you're out there working around heavy machinery all day, you have to be so careful. You have to know if you're getting too fatigued, or if the heat is getting to you, or if you're just not sharp enough that afternoon. Because a single mistake out there on the fog line means someone could get clipped by a dump truck or hit by some commuter who's too busy looking at their phone to see the bright orange warning signs. So I am always running a sort of internal diagnostic check, I guess you could say. I'm constantly taking inventory of how I feel. 

And because I'm paying such close attention, I can tell you with absolute certainty that I haven't experienced whatever it is you're describing. It really is just this one specific, terrifying issue where my brain just stops processing my job tasks. Aside from that, I don't have any of these other things you're asking about. Just the blankness. I hope that makes sense, and I know it probably feels like I'm just shooting down all your questions today, but I really just want to give you the exact, accurate picture of what's happening to me out there on the pavement. So, no, I haven't noticed anything like that.

No, I haven't. Honestly, I'm pretty sure I would have noticed if something like that was going on. My routine is incredibly structured, almost to a fault. I mean, I have a bachelor's degree—I didn't exactly plan on spending my early forties standing on a highway holding a stop sign next to a paving crew, but life happens, you know? You take the work that pays the bills, and you just get into a rhythm. 

When you work a job like mine, out in the elements for ten or twelve hours a day, you really rely on that strict routine just to survive the week. I get up at the exact same time every single morning, I pack the exact same lunch—usually a turkey sandwich and an apple, because it holds up in the heat—and I go stand on my designated patch of gravel. By the time I get home, I'm so physically drained that I just take a hot shower and collapse. There isn't really any room in my day for anything else to go wrong. 

So no, I haven't experienced anything like what you're asking about. It really just comes back to those terrifying moments where my brain completely empties out on the job site. That is the one and only thing that's out of the ordinary for me. Everything else is just my normal, everyday grind.

Can you tell me roughly how often these blank spells are happening now—like, how many times a day or week—and whether that frequency has been getting better, worse, or staying about the same over the past year and eight months?

Well, it's... it's hard to put an exact number on it, but it's definitely happening more often. When it first started, maybe a year and a half ago, it was just every once in a while. I'd be out there on a Friday afternoon, completely exhausted, the sun beating down on the asphalt, and I'd just have a momentary lapse. I brushed it off as fatigue. I mean, anyone would, right? Standing on blacktop in ninety-degree heat for twelve hours will fry anyone's brain. But then it started creeping into other days. A Tuesday morning. A Thursday right after lunch. 

Now? Now it's happening almost every single shift. Sometimes multiple times a day. And it's not just a quick stutter-step anymore. It's like... I came in because my mind just keeps going completely blank at the absolute worst times. I'll be standing there, the crew will be relying on me to manage the flow, and I'll look down at the road-closure forms on my clipboard, or I'll look at the stop-slow paddle in my hands, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps. The steps I have done for years. It's like someone just unplugs the machine. I know what the paddle is, I know I'm at work, but the actual sequence of thoughts required to do the job just vanishes. 

Last week, we were setting up a lane closure on Route 9, and I had the radio in one hand and the paddle in the other, and a pilot car was coming through. All I had to do was flip the sign to 'Stop' and radio the other flagger to let the queue go. Simple, right? I've done it ten thousand times. But I just stood there. The pilot car driver was staring at me, the foreman was yelling over the noise of the milling machine, and my brain was just... empty. It was terrifying. I felt so stupid, so useless. And it's just getting worse. It used to be a rare glitch, and now it feels like I'm constantly waiting for the floor to drop out from under me. I can't keep working like this, I really can't. It's too dangerous.

We went through so much together during college, and even after, when we were both just trying to figure out what to do with our degrees. Losing her... it was devastating. It still is. patient.answer:
Well, see, I’ve spent a lot of time trying to figure that out myself. Because you'd think it would be stress, right? Road work is inherently stressful. But it doesn't really feel like I'm having a particularly anxious day and *then* it happens. It's more like... it just happens at the absolute worst possible times, almost like a cruel joke. 

And honestly, that is the whole reason I finally made this appointment and came in here to see you. Because my mind just keeps going completely blank at the exact moments I need it to work the most. Like, I will be looking at the daily road-closure forms—and these are standard forms, I have filled them out literally hundreds of times. With my background, you'd think a simple closure form wouldn't be an issue, and it never was before. But I'll be staring at the clipboard, or I'll be out there holding the stop-slow paddle, just doing the routine, and suddenly... I just cannot remember the steps. Steps I have done for years! 

It’s all just wiped clean. I’m standing there staring at the paperwork, or staring at this piece of reflective aluminum on a stick, trying to force my brain to remember what comes next, and the knowledge is just... not there. And that *causes* stress, obviously. When you're standing there and the foreman needs the forms signed off so the concrete trucks can move, or when you have a line of commuters tapping their steering wheels, you feel the pressure. But the anxiety comes *after* the blankness, not before. 

Before it happens, I'm usually just doing my job. I'm just existing. And then, bam, the instructions are gone. It's so incredibly frustrating because it makes me look incompetent to the rest of the crew, and I'm not. I've been doing this for years. So I guess to answer your question, the blankness itself seems to just hit me randomly, regardless of how I'm feeling. It just always manages to pick the exact moment I can least afford for it to happen.

inference.note: Absence of automatisms, postictal confusion, or observed unresponsiveness makes classic seizure activity less typical, while preserved full awareness during 'blank' spells continues to favor a dissociative/functional process; retaining both pending EEG or further episode detail.

doctor.intent: Determine if there's any postictal confusion, fatigue, or need for recovery time after the episodes resolve, which would suggest a seizure-like process versus a dissociative one
doctor.question: After one of these blank spells ends and your mind 'clicks back on,' do you feel completely normal right away, or do you feel tired, foggy, or need a little time to fully get back to yourself?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the recovery period after the blank spells, specifically looking for signs of a postictal state (like fatigue or fogginess) to rule out seizures, which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, no, it’s completely immediate. There’s no fog, no tiredness, nothing like that at all. It’s literally just... boom, I’m back. Like I said before with the old TV analogy, once the picture is there, it’s just there in full color. I don't need to sit down or splash water on my face or take a minute to get my bearings. 

Which is a good thing, honestly, because out on the road, you really don't have the luxury of taking a minute. If you're foggy out there, if you're sluggish, somebody gets run over or a cement truck backs into a trench. So when I snap back, I am instantly at a hundred percent again. Like with that lady in the silver Honda I was telling you about... the very second my brain plugged back in and I remembered I was holding the paddle, I didn't feel groggy in the slightest. I just instantly flipped the sign from 'stop' to 'slow' and gave her the wave to move forward. Now, my heart was pounding, sure, but that was just from the sheer panic of realizing I had been standing there like a statue, not because my body was physically exhausted or my head was cloudy. 

It’s the exact same thing with the closure forms. One second I'm staring at the clipboard like it's written in ancient Greek, and the next second, the English language just returns to my brain and I sign the bottom line and hand it back to the foreman. I don't need a nap, I don't have a headache, my vision isn't blurry. I just pick up exactly where I left off. 

It's almost more jarring that way, to be honest with you. Because if I felt tired or sick afterward, at least I'd have a tangible excuse, right? I could tell the crew, "Oh, man, I'm feeling really under the weather today, I got dizzy for a second," and they'd understand. But I don't. I feel completely fine physically. I'm just standing there in my high-vis vest, totally alert, perfectly awake, just... trying to seamlessly re-enter the flow of traffic and pretend like I wasn't just completely checked out of my own head. And I'll tell you, that takes a lot of mental energy, having to constantly cover up the fact that my brain keeps dropping the signal. But the actual physical feeling right after it happens? No, no fog at all. I'm just instantly back to normal.

inference.note: The lack of automatisms, preserved full awareness during episodes, absence of any postictal confusion or fatigue, and immediate 'snap back' to baseline make a seizure disorder (G40.9) unlikely, so it has been ruled out. The clinical picture—episodic loss of procedural/cognitive access with intact consciousness and no autonomic arousal—remains most consistent with a dissociative process.

patient.answer:
Well... yes. I’ve actually spent a lot of time trying to trace it all back to day one, trying to figure out exactly when the switch flipped. Because you always want to know where things begin, right? If you can find the source of a leak, maybe you can figure out how to patch it. So I’ve gone over the timeline in my head a thousand times, looking at the calendar, looking back at my old work schedules and trying to pinpoint the exact moment my brain started doing this. 

And it’s been going on for about a year and eight months now. And the reason I know that timeline so specifically, down to the month, is because of what happened right before it all started. You asked about a loss, and... yeah. My closest friend died. Just right before all this blankness began. 

We were incredibly close. We actually met back when I was getting my bachelor's degree, and we had been through everything together since then. You know how you have that one person who just anchors you? The person who just inherently understands how your mind works? When you lose that, the whole world just shifts on its axis. I remember the exact season she passed, because the road crew was just transitioning into the fall paving schedule, and I had to take time off for the funeral. It was just devastating. 

And when I finally came back to work after that... that's when I first noticed the signal dropping in my head. The blank spells. It's been a year and eight months of this, and honestly, it feels like an absolute eternity to be dealing with this on top of everything else. But at the same time, the loss feels like it just happened yesterday. The grief just lingers, it sits heavy right on your chest, you know? And I keep thinking, maybe if she were still here, I wouldn't be standing on the highway forgetting how to read a standard closure form. Because she was always the one I talked to to decompress after a long shift. When she passed away, it left this massive, gaping hole in my life that nothing else can fill. 

So, yes, a year and eight months. Right after I lost her. I really think the two things have to be connected, because the timing is just too perfectly aligned for it to be a coincidence. I mean, one week my life is normal, the next week she's gone, and then suddenly my brain is just hitting the pause button on me. It has to be related to losing her, it just has to be.

patient.answer:
No, I... I wouldn't say that. Not like what you're describing. Like, with the sleeping thing? My sleep is always kind of all over the place anyway, just by the very nature of the job. When you're a flagger, you're completely at the mercy of the construction schedule. Sometimes we have night work because the city won't let them shut down the highway during peak daylight traffic hours, so I'll be out there from 9 PM to 5 AM standing under those massive, blinding halogen light towers. And then two weeks later, I'll get moved to a residential paving job that strictly runs 7 AM to 3 PM because of local noise ordinances. So my internal clock has been completely wrecked for years. If I have trouble falling asleep, it's usually just because my body literally doesn't know what time it is, not because I'm lying awake having nightmares or anything like that. 

And as far as avoiding places... no, definitely not. Honestly, it's almost the exact opposite. We lived in the same city for so long, we went to school together, so practically every square inch of this town has some kind of memory attached to it. If I started avoiding places that reminded me of her, I literally wouldn't be able to leave my apartment. I'd have to quit my job, because we used to drive these same roads all the time. Actually, I still go to the diner we used to eat at every single Sunday. It's this little place off Route 9, nothing fancy at all, but they have the best hash browns. We used to sit in the exact same booth in the back corner by the window. I still go there, and I still sit in that same booth. The waitress, Brenda, she still gives me this really sad, sympathetic smile when she brings the coffee because she knows I'm there alone now. But I don't avoid it. It actually feels nice to be there, in a way. 

So I don't really have those... what did you call them, intrusive memories? It's not like a sudden flashback or something jarring that forces its way into my head and scares me. It's not like that at all. It's just a constant, quiet missing her. It's just a heavy feeling that's always sort of sitting there. I'll be out on the road, holding my sign, and I'll see a car that looks like hers, or I'll hear a song on a passing car's radio that we used to listen to, and I just feel sad. But it doesn't interrupt my thoughts or make me panic or anything. It's really just these blank spells, where the signal just completely shuts off. That's the only really bizarre thing that's been happening. Everything else is just... you know, normal grief, I guess you'd call it. Just trying to figure out how to exist in a daily routine where she isn't around anymore. But no, no avoiding things or sudden bad memories keeping me awake.

inference.note: Grief symptoms described are typical/uncomplicated, without intrusive memories, avoidance, or sleep disturbance beyond job-related circadian issues, ruling out PTSD (F43.1) and reducing likelihood of adjustment disorder. Absence of automatisms, autonomic symptoms, or post-episode confusion further argues against a seizure disorder. Episodes remain consistent with stress/grief-related dissociative blocking (F44.89) or an atypical stress-reaction pattern (F43.8) tied temporally to bereavement.

But the whole reason I actually came in here to see you, the reason I finally picked up the phone and made this appointment, is because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst possible times. Like, the highest-stakes moments you could possibly imagine. I know I already brought up the road-closure forms and the stop-slow paddle earlier, but you really have to understand the context of it. I have been doing this job for years. Years. It is pure muscle memory at this point. You stand there, you flip the paddle, you make eye contact with the driver, you wave them through. But then, out of nowhere, I will look at the road-closure forms or the stop-slow paddle, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I have done for years. It's like someone just reached into my brain and wiped the hard drive completely clean. I'll just be standing there on the asphalt, looking at this piece of paper or holding this sign, and for the life of me, I have absolutely no idea what it means or what I'm supposed to do next. The knowledge just completely evaporates. 

And when you're standing in a live lane of traffic, with a line of cars stretching back a quarter mile, and people are getting impatient and leaning on their horns... that is not the time to forget how to do your job. It's terrifying, honestly. It's a massive liability. So, maybe it happens at home, I really couldn't say for sure because there's no pressure there to snap me out of it or make me notice. But the work stuff? That's why I'm here. Because forgetting the most basic steps of my job while I'm standing in the middle of a highway... I just can't keep trying to hide that.

No, I... I don't think so. I mean, I know what you're talking about, like in movies when someone goes through something intense and they suddenly float up to the ceiling and look down at themselves, or everything goes all blurry and slow-motion? It's really not like that at all. I am very, very much in my own body. 

If anything, I'm almost hyper-aware of being in my body because I'm standing there panicking on the inside. I can feel the exact weight of my steel-toe boots, you know? I can feel the sweat dripping down the back of my neck under my hard hat, and I can smell the diesel exhaust from the excavators, and that really sharp, chemical smell of the hot mix asphalt... it's all incredibly real. Too real, honestly. The world doesn't feel like a dream at all. The cars flying past me at sixty miles an hour definitely don't feel like a dream—the wind they kick up practically knocks you over if you aren't bracing your legs right. 

So I'm definitely grounded right there on the pavement. It's just... it's more like a computer freezing up. You know when you're working on something and suddenly the screen just stops responding, but the monitor is still on and the power is still connected and you can see everything perfectly fine, but you just can't click on anything? That's what it is. I'm looking right out of my own two eyes, and everything around me is sharp and loud and exactly where it should be, but the... the internal mechanism that tells me what to do next just completely halts. So, no, definitely no floating around or feeling disconnected from reality. I'm right there in the dirt and the noise. I just... I just don't know what I'm supposed to be doing while I'm standing there.

No, God, I wish there was. I really, really wish there was some kind of warning, because if there was, maybe I could actually do something about it, you know? If I had even a five-second heads-up, I could step back from the fog line, or I could grab my radio and tell the other flagger, "Hey, cover my lane for a second, I need to step away." But I don't get that luxury. 

You asked about smells or tastes... I mean, out on the highway, you smell absolutely everything all day long. You smell the fresh hot tar, the diesel exhaust from the dump trucks, someone's burning brake pads coming down the hill, or just the stale coffee in my own thermos. It's a sensory overload out there. But there's never any *strange* smell right before it happens, or any weird taste in my mouth. It's just the normal, everyday smells of a heavy construction zone right up until the exact second my brain decides to pull the plug. 

And as for déjà vu? No, not at all. Honestly, it's almost the exact opposite of déjà vu. Because déjà vu is when you feel like you've been somewhere or done something before, right? But with this, it's like... I *have* been there a thousand times. I've stood on that exact patch of asphalt all week. But when the blank spell hits, suddenly it's like I've *never* been there. It's not a warning sign, it's just the spell itself hitting me like a ton of bricks. 

There's just no build-up whatsoever. One second I'm totally fine, I'm watching a silver Honda Civic coming up the lane, I'm calculating their speed, I'm checking my footing on the gravel, I'm thinking about whether I need to flip the paddle to 'Stop' or keep it on 'Slow' based on what the pilot car is doing... and the very next second, nothing. Just a totally empty room in my head. No weird tingling, no stomach dropping, no sudden chill. It's literally just like a light switch being flipped off without anyone even touching the dial. Which is exactly why it's so incredibly dangerous! If I just had a warning, I could manage it. But because there's absolutely nothing tipping me off... I'm just completely at its mercy out there.
